name: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church — Suppression and Return

items.quote: Decree 358 of 1 December 1948 dissolved the Romanian Greek Catholic Church.
items.heart: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church was dissolved in 1948, had no legal existence for forty-one years, and was restored in 1989.

items.quote: On 31 December 1989 Decree-Law 9 restored it.
items.heart: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church was dissolved in 1948, had no legal existence for forty-one years, and was restored in 1989.

items.quote: a new translation split the four Gospels apart again
items.heart: The woven Gospel was replaced by separate Gospels after 410, and its Syriac text was lost.
items.why: The heart rests on the woven Gospel being replaced, and the piece never says why the new translation split the Gospels apart.

items.quote: Bacon, a later editor of Luther's hymns, notes a detail of the same book, the 1524 "Eight Songs."
items.heart: Wittenberg's first hymn-book of 1524 held Speratus's hymn, and a tradition says a wanderer sang it beneath Luther's window.
items.why: Bacon is a later editor named in the text, and his note takes up one of the piece's three paragraphs.

items.quote: Bacon's Introduction also relates a tradition about the hymn.
items.heart: Wittenberg's first hymn-book of 1524 held Speratus's hymn, and a tradition says a wanderer sang it beneath Luther's window.
items.why: The tradition about the wanderer, which is half the heart, reaches the listener through a modern editor's Introduction.

name: Philippine Catholicism in the Twentieth Century

items.quote: El Shaddai grew up within the same church.
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism clashed with the Marcos regime and then took part in civil society, with El Shaddai as a change in popular Catholicism.

items.quote: Robert Youngblood followed that clash in Marcos against the Church (1990).
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism after 1906 is told through the church's clash with Marcos, its part in civil society, and El Shaddai, mostly as modern authors studied them.
items.why: The heart says the clash with Marcos is told as modern authors studied it, and Youngblood is the one telling it.

items.quote: He tied it to the regime's drive for economic growth.
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism after 1906 is told through the church's clash with Marcos, its part in civil society, and El Shaddai, mostly as modern authors studied them.
items.why: Youngblood's modern reading of what drove the clash is reported as his interpretation of a central strand.

items.quote: He tied it to its political repression too.
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism after 1906 is told through the church's clash with Marcos, its part in civil society, and El Shaddai, mostly as modern authors studied them.
items.why: This is the second half of the same modern reading of the Marcos clash, given equal place.

items.quote: Afterward the Filipino Jesuit Antonio Moreno studied the church's part in civil society.
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism after 1906 is told through the church's clash with Marcos, its part in civil society, and El Shaddai, mostly as modern authors studied them.
items.why: Moreno, a modern scholar, is the only way the piece tells of the church's part in civil society, which the heart rests on.

items.quote: Katharine Wiegele studied it as a change in popular Catholicism.
items.heart: Philippine Catholicism after 1906 is told through the church's clash with Marcos, its part in civil society, and El Shaddai, mostly as modern authors studied them.
items.why: Wiegele, a modern scholar, is the only way the piece presents El Shaddai, which the heart names.

items.quote: Historians date the popular liturgical movement from that address.

items.heart: The liturgical movement began with Beauduin's 1909 address, spread through journals in America and England, and tied worship to social life.

items.quote: Hebert's collection The Parish Communion (1937) set out a practice that changed the pattern of Sunday-morning worship.
items.asks: What practice, and how did it change worship?
items.heart: The liturgical movement began with Beauduin's 1909 address, spread through journals in America and England, and tied worship to social life.
items.why: The piece never names the practice or how it changed Sunday worship.

items.quote: In England, Gabriel Hebert published Liturgy and Society in 1935.
items.heart: The liturgical movement began with Beauduin's 1909 address, spread through journals in America and England, and tied worship to social life.
items.why: The book's reception is given but nothing of what it says.

items.quote: Historians date the popular liturgical movement from that address.
items.heart: The liturgical movement ran from Beauduin's 1909 address through Virgil Michel's journal and Gabriel Hebert's Parish Communion, tying worship to common life.
items.why: The heart says the movement ran from Beauduin's 1909 address, and the only support for that starting point is "Historians date".

items.quote: Keith Pecklers showed how closely its American leaders tied worship to social justice in the 1930s and 1940s.
items.heart: The liturgical movement ran from Beauduin's 1909 address through Virgil Michel's journal and Gabriel Hebert's Parish Communion, tying worship to common life.
items.why: A modern scholar is named as the support for the tie between worship and social life, which is half of the heart.

items.quote: argue in vocabulary this circle fought to place
items.heart: The Cappadocian teachers' vocabulary shaped later Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teaching, though historians dispute whether they shared one scheme.
items.why: The piece never says what vocabulary this circle fought to place.

items.quote: Did the three teachers ever share one settled scheme
items.heart: The Cappadocian teachers' vocabulary shaped later Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teaching, though historians dispute whether they shared one scheme.
items.why: The disputed "settled scheme" is never said to be about anything in particular, though the heart rests on that dispute.

items.quote: Even the letter most often cited to prove their agreement is in doubt
items.heart: The Cappadocians' vocabulary shaped later churches, though historians now dispute whether the three shared one settled scheme.
items.why: The letter is not named and the piece gives no word of what it says.

items.quote: Historians now dispute this.
items.heart: The Cappadocian teachers' words became curriculum, liturgy and law for later churches, though whether they shared one settled scheme is disputed.
items.why: "Historians now dispute this" is the dispute the heart itself names.

items.quote: Even the letter most often cited to prove their agreement is in doubt, since many scholars now think it was written not by Basil but by his brother Gregory.
items.heart: The Cappadocian teachers' words became curriculum, liturgy and law for later churches, though whether they shared one settled scheme is disputed.
items.why: "Many scholars now think" a modern reattribution, and it backs the dispute the piece spends its second paragraph on.

name: The Union of Brest & Ruthenian Greek Catholic Christianity

items.quote: accepted communion with Rome
items.asks: Why did the bishops do this?
items.heart: At Brest in 1596 most Orthodox bishops joined Rome while keeping their rites, and their opponents rejected the union. Two rival hierarchies resulted.

items.quote: rejected it outright
items.asks: Why did their opponents reject it?
items.heart: At Brest in 1596 most Orthodox bishops joined Rome while keeping their rites, and their opponents rejected the union. Two rival hierarchies resulted.

items.quote: was killed by a hostile crowd at Vitebsk in 1623
items.heart: At Brest in 1596 most Orthodox bishops joined Rome while keeping their rites, and their opponents rejected the union. Two rival hierarchies resulted.

items.quote: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens traced one root of homeschooling to the Christian day-school movement of the 1960s and 1970s.
items.heart: Homeschooling grew from the Christian day-school movement and the Moores' ideas, and organized in 1983 with the Home School Legal Defense Association.
items.why: The heart's claim that homeschooling grew from the day-school movement rests on sociologist Stevens's tracing.

items.quote: Alan Peshkin spent eighteen months in one such school, a Baptist school in Illinois, in the late 1970s. He called it a 'total world'.
items.heart: Homeschooling grew from the Christian day-school movement and the Moores' ideas, and organized in 1983 with the Home School Legal Defense Association.
items.why: Peshkin is a modern scholar whose fieldwork and label are cited along the way.

items.quote: A reviewer of Stevens's study summed the movement up as 'a woman's enterprise, in which men are usually junior partners'.
items.heart: Homeschooling grew from the Christian day-school movement and the Moores' ideas, and organized in 1983 with the Home School Legal Defense Association.
items.why: A modern reviewer's summary of the movement is quoted in the closing line, in passing.

items.quote: Rome condemned it as heretical again and again
items.heart: The Bosnian church was an independent, disputed church whose beliefs remain uncertain, and which ended with the kingdom.
items.why: Rome's charge of heresy is never stated (the Bogomil view is given as a historians' reading, not as Rome's charge), and the heart rests on disputed belief.

items.quote: What its members actually believed is still in real dispute.
items.heart: The Bosnian church was a protected, condemned church whose beliefs are disputed, with one inside document, Gost Radin's will.
items.why: The live modern dispute over what the members believed is exactly what the heart says.

items.quote: Since the 1970s most historians have rejected the long-held view that they were Bogomil dualists.
items.heart: The Bosnian church was a protected, condemned church whose beliefs are disputed, with one inside document, Gost Radin's will.
items.why: "Most historians" since the 1970s is a modern consensus, and it gives substance to the dispute the heart names.

items.quote: Modern research, above all Robert Lerner's study of 1972, concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed.
items.heart: The church declared in 1312 that a Free Spirit sect existed, but the sect may have been a charge laid on a wide range of mystical piety.
items.why: Lerner's 1972 study is modern research, and the heart's claim that the sect may not have existed rests on it.

items.quote: The movement named here probably was not real; the charge and its victims certainly were.
items.heart: The church declared in 1312 that a Free Spirit sect existed, but the sect may have been a charge laid on a wide range of mystical piety.
items.why: "Probably was not real" is a reconstruction told as part of the story, and the heart rests on it.

items.quote: what they worked out together became the Consensus Tigurinus
items.heart: In 1549 Calvin went to Zurich to settle fears that the two churches taught different things about the Supper. The result was the Consensus Tigurinus.

items.quote: Calvin's teaching on the Supper differed from what Zurich taught
items.asks: What did each church teach about the Supper?
items.heart: In 1549 Calvin went to Zurich to settle fears that the two churches taught different things about the Supper. The result was the Consensus Tigurinus.
items.why: The piece names the Supper as the subject of the feared difference but never says what the difference was thought to be.

items.quote: No single morning like this was written down, so this one is pieced together from separate sources
items.heart: Before dawn in Nisibis the covenanters gather for the vigil and the singing of the teaching hymn.
items.why: The piece says the whole morning, which is the heart itself, is pieced together, so the reconstruction is the story.

items.quote: after the violence of 1965 and 1966
items.asks: What violence, and who did it to whom?
items.heart: Indonesian churches ran themselves for most of the twentieth century, had a disputed revival on Timor, and grew fast after 1965 in a way tied to its context.
items.why: The piece never says what the violence was, yet the heart ties the growth of the churches to that context.

items.quote: is disputed for embellishment
items.who: unnamed disputers of Mel Tari's account
items.heart: Indonesian churches became independent early, and two turning points, the Timor revival and the post-1965 growth, are hard to tell apart from their context.
items.why: A modern dispute over Tari's account is told as settled background, and it carries the heart's claim that the Timor revival is hard to tell apart.

items.quote: whose most careful evaluation, George W. Peters's Indonesia Revival: Focus on Timor (1973), was written on the ground
items.heart: Indonesian churches became independent early, and two turning points, the Timor revival and the post-1965 growth, are hard to tell apart from their context.
items.why: A modern scholar's book is named and judged "most careful", which passes on the way to the Timor point.

items.quote: a growth that cannot honestly be told apart from its context
items.heart: Indonesian churches became independent early, and two turning points, the Timor revival and the post-1965 growth, are hard to tell apart from their context.
items.why: The narrator's own judgment that the growth cannot honestly be told apart from its context is the very claim the heart rests on.

items.quote: it lost its independent standing, when its catholicos was placed under the Armenian church
items.asks: Why was the catholicos placed under Armenia?
items.heart: Caucasian Albania was a third Caucasian Christian kingdom that left little behind, lost its independence in the early 700s, and was recovered through Sinai palimpsests.
items.why: The piece says the catholicos was placed under the Armenian church but not by whom or why, and the heart rests on this loss of independence.

items.quote: Whether the line is original, or was added later by another hand, is not settled.
items.heart: The Chronicle of Edessa records the flood of about 201 and, in one line, the destruction of a church of the Christians.
items.why: The open question of whether the line is original is a modern textual judgment about the one line the heart rests on.

items.quote: If it is original, a church building stood in Edessa to be destroyed, and that line is the earliest hard trace of a church there.
items.heart: The Chronicle of Edessa records the flood of about 201 and, in one line, the destruction of a church of the Christians.
items.why: The conditional "if it is original" and "earliest hard trace" are modern reasoning about what the line shows, and the piece's central paragraph spends real time on it.

items.quote: in 645 he debated the ousted patriarch Pyrrhus in Africa
items.heart: After Belisarius, the African church stubbornly resisted Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters and later compromises, until Arab conquest ended it.

items.quote: When he condemned the Three Chapters to appease the Miaphysites
items.asks: What are the Three Chapters, and why did Africa refuse?
items.heart: The African church, restored after Vandal rule, stubbornly resisted Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters and later compromises until Arab conquest ended it.
items.why: The heart rests on resistance to condemning the Three Chapters, yet the piece never says what they were or why condemning them would appease anyone.

items.quote: the empire's next bid for a compromise on the wills of Christ
items.heart: The African church, restored after Vandal rule, stubbornly resisted Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters and later compromises until Arab conquest ended it.
items.why: The compromise the councils threw out is named only as a "bid" on the wills of Christ, with no word of what it proposed.

name: Hugeburc Signs Her Name in Code

items.quote: in 1931 Bernhard Bischoff decoded it
items.heart: Hugeburc, a nun, wrote down Willibald's pilgrimage and hid her own name in a line of coded letters.
items.why: A modern scholar, Bischoff, is named as decoding the line, and her hidden name, which the heart rests on, is known only through his reading.

items.quote: Every one of the church's bishops had already been arrested, and none took part.
items.heart: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church was dissolved into the Russian Orthodox Church in 1946, survived underground for forty-three years, and emerged intact in 1989.
items.why: The bishops' arrest is stated with no reason or charge given anywhere in the piece.

items.quote: a synod was convened at Lviv that dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church
items.asks: Why did the state want the church dissolved?
items.heart: The Soviet state dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church in 1946, and it survived underground for forty-three years and came out in 1989 intact.
items.why: The piece never says who convened the Lviv synod or why the church was dissolved, and the heart rests on that dissolution.

items.quote: the Greek Catholic Church was liquidated between 1948 and 1950
items.heart: The Soviet state dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church in 1946, and it survived underground for forty-three years and came out in 1989 intact.
items.why: The Czechoslovak liquidation and "Action P" are given with no word of who carried them out or why.

items.quote: is now widely judged unreliable in its details
items.who: unnamed (wide modern judgment of the Panarion)
items.heart: Jewish believers in Jesus kept the Law, and we know them only through hostile and disagreeing later writers, so their identity is unclear.
items.why: "Now widely judged unreliable" is a modern scholarly verdict that backs the piece's case that the hostile sources are weak.

items.quote: And modern scholars genuinely disagree about whether 'Ebionite' and 'Nazoraean' name two distinct groups, one group under two labels, or largely a category the heresy-hunters assembled.
items.heart: Jewish believers in Jesus kept the Law, and we know them only through hostile and disagreeing later writers, so their identity is unclear.
items.why: The modern scholars' disagreement is what the heart's "their identity is unclear" rests on.

items.quote: he was summoned to Augsburg
items.heart: Luther, remembering years later, told how he went before Cardinal Cajetan in 1518, knelt, and refused to recant.

items.quote: say one word, Revoco, which means I recant
items.heart: Luther, remembering years later, told how he went before Cardinal Cajetan in 1518, knelt, and refused to recant.
items.why: The piece never says what Luther was being pressed to recant, and his refusal is the heart.

items.quote: would not recant anything
items.heart: Luther, urged to say "I recant", knelt before Cardinal Cajetan but refused to recant, and said he was safe "under Heaven".
items.why: The refusal to recant comes with no word of which teaching was at stake, and the heart rests on that refusal.

items.quote: Which tells us the intervening centuries were not empty, only silent.
items.heart: Ethiopian Christianity went quiet for five hundred years but survived, as the later record shows.
items.why: The narrator's own inference, that the silent centuries were not empty, is told as the story's conclusion, and the heart rests on it.

items.quote: the Donatist rule did not hold even for the Donatists themselves
items.heart: Donatist bishops harshly condemned the Maximianist split, then took back two condemned bishops, which Augustine used to argue the Donatist rule failed by their own practice.
items.why: This piece never states what "the Donatist rule" was, yet Augustine's whole argument, and the heart, turn on it.

items.quote: took back two of those condemned bishops
items.asks: Why did they take back men they had just condemned?
items.heart: The Donatists condemned the followers of Maximian harshly at Bagai, then took two of the condemned bishops back, which Augustine used to argue the Donatist rule failed by their own practice.
items.why: The piece never says why the Donatists took back two bishops they had just condemned so harshly.

items.quote: a deacon named Maximian was made rival primate at Cebarsussi
items.asks: Why was he made rival primate?
items.heart: The Donatists condemned the followers of Maximian harshly at Bagai, then took two of the condemned bishops back, which Augustine used to argue the Donatist rule failed by their own practice.
items.why: The piece never says why Maximian was set up against Primian, so the split has no subject.

items.quote: it took a two-century scholarly fight to settle which of his letters were genuine.
items.heart: The single-bishop pattern won out, and which texts survived depended on what a later settlement found useful, not on what mattered most at the time.
items.why: A two-century scholarly fight is modern scholarship, told within the piece's account of which texts survived.

items.quote: Some scholars still doubt them.
items.heart: The single-bishop pattern won out, and which texts survived depended on what a later settlement found useful, not on what mattered most at the time.
items.why: "Some scholars" refers to modern scholars directly, in a brief aside.

items.quote: That was a real demotion, though not the outright ban later memory sometimes assumes.
items.heart: The single-bishop pattern won out, and which texts survived depended on what a later settlement found useful, not on what mattered most at the time.
items.why: Calling it a real demotion and not the ban later memory assumes is a modern corrective judgment, made in passing on Hermas.

items.quote: It may have been what a later settlement found useful to keep.
items.heart: The single-bishop pattern won out, and which texts survived depended on what a later settlement found useful, not on what mattered most at the time.
items.why: "It may have been" is a guess, and the heart's claim about why texts survived rests on it.

items.quote: The letter's closing lines seemed to prove it.
items.asks: What did the closing lines say?
items.heart: The Donatist charge that Felix had handed over the scriptures was tried before the proconsul, who found a forged letter and cleared Felix.
items.why: The piece never says what the letter's closing lines said, and the forged letter is what the heart rests on.

name: Polish and Lithuanian Catholicism Under the Partitions

items.quote: Bismarck began his conflict with the Church.
items.heart: Under Russian and Prussian rule after the partitions, the Catholic Church in Poland and Lithuania was suppressed and persecuted, yet the clergy held their ground until toleration came after 1905.

items.quote: After the three partitions, Russia tried to destroy the Catholic Church as well as Polish nationality, says the Catholic Encyclopedia.
items.heart: Under the partitions Russia and Prussia pressed the Catholic Church in Poland and Lithuania, closing convents and seizing property, while the clergy held their ground until the toleration edict.
items.why: The Catholic Encyclopedia, a modern work, is the source the whole piece rests on, starting with its charge that Russia meant to destroy the church.

items.quote: After it, the article says, Uniats were forced to give up their faith.
items.heart: Under the partitions Russia and Prussia pressed the Catholic Church in Poland and Lithuania, closing convents and seizing property, while the clergy held their ground until the toleration edict.
items.why: "The article says" ties the forced conversions after 1831 to the modern encyclopedia, a part the piece spends real time on.

items.quote: Prussia treated its Catholic Poles no better, the article says.
items.heart: Under the partitions Russia and Prussia pressed the Catholic Church in Poland and Lithuania, closing convents and seizing property, while the clergy held their ground until the toleration edict.
items.why: "The article says" ties the Prussian half of the story to the modern encyclopedia, a part the piece spends real time on.

name: The Emperor Turned Away at the Door on Christmas Day (in The Byzantine Imperial Church (Macedonian Era))

items.quote: The imperial church of the Macedonian age is often described as the emperor’s creature
items.heart: Patriarch Nicholas barred Leo VI from Hagia Sophia over his fourth marriage, showing the church was not simply the emperor's creature.
items.why: "Often described as" brings in an unnamed body of modern opinion, and the heart's point that the church was not simply the emperor's creature is set against it.

name: Servetus at Champel, and Castellio’s Answer (in Anti-Trinitarian Currents (Servetus; Polish Brethren/Socinians; Transylvanian Unitarians))

items.quote: Calvin drew up the charges and argued the theology
items.asks: What were the charges and what was the theology?
items.heart: Calvin's Geneva burned Servetus in 1553, and Castellio answered with a defense of toleration.

items.quote: had been condemned for the Christianismi Restitutio
items.asks: What did the book say that got him condemned?
items.heart: Calvin's Geneva burned Servetus in 1553, and Castellio answered with a defense of toleration.

items.quote: Beza answered him
items.heart: Servetus was burned at Geneva for his teaching, and Castellio answered with an argument against killing for doctrine.
items.why: Beza's answer is reported with no word of what it argued.

name: Two Million in Six Years (in Indonesian Christianity — the Independent Century)

items.quote: a group of army officers killed six generals in Jakarta
items.asks: Why did they kill the generals?
items.heart: After the 1965 massacres and a state demand that everyone hold a religion, about two million Indonesians entered the churches, and the churches admitted the mixed reasons.
items.why: The officers kill six generals, and the piece gives no reason for the killings.

items.quote: something like two million people had entered the churches across Indonesia
items.heart: After the 1965 killings, churches took in huge numbers of people in a state that required a religion, and the churches themselves told the whole context.
items.why: "Something like two million" is a modern estimate told as part of the story, and it is the piece's main measure of the huge numbers, which "tens of thousands a year" also carries.

items.quote: Estimates of the dead run from five hundred thousand to a million
items.heart: After the 1965 killings, churches took in huge numbers of people in a state that required a religion, and the churches themselves told the whole context.
items.why: "Estimates of the dead" refers to modern reckonings, given in passing as background to the heart.

items.quote: Missionary writers called it revival; Indonesian church historians insisted on the whole context, and the churches themselves largely adopted that honesty.
items.who: missionary writers and Indonesian church historians, unnamed
items.heart: After the 1965 killings, churches took in huge numbers of people in a state that required a religion, and the churches themselves told the whole context.
items.why: The piece names "missionary writers" and "Indonesian church historians", and the heart's claim that the churches told the whole context rests on this sentence.

name: The Night at Soe (in Indonesian Christianity — the Independent Century)

items.quote: the attempted coup in Jakarta that would change the country
items.heart: A 1965 revival at Soe on Timor sent out lay teams, and an outside missiologist later judged the awakening genuine but many spectacular claims unsupported.
items.why: The coup "would change the country", but the piece never says what it was or how it changed things.

items.quote: In 1972 George Peters, a missiologist from Dallas, spent weeks on Timor interviewing team members, pastors and villagers. His book of 1973 concluded that a genuine and lasting awakening had occurred, that the testimony of changed lives and burned fetishes was overwhelming, and that many of the spectacular claims did not survive questioning of the people said to have witnessed them.
items.heart: A 1965 service at Soe began a Timor revival, and a later missiologist's study found real awakening but doubted the spectacular claims.
items.why: George Peters is a modern missiologist, and the heart rests on his study's conclusions.

name: Vasak Siwni, the Man the Tradition Needed to Blame (in Armenian Christianity after Avarayr)

items.quote: Modern historians have noted that Vasak’s policy of accommodation was the one Armenia actually adopted after 484, when Vahan Mamikonian negotiated the right to remain Christian under Persian rule, and that Vasak’s crime in the tradition’s eyes was less what he did than that he did it too soon and without a martyr’s death to redeem it.
items.heart: Elishe made Vasak Siwni the villain of Avarayr, while his policy was in the end the one Armenia adopted.
items.why: "Modern historians have noted" carries the heart's claim that Vasak's policy was the one Armenia adopted.

name: Tarbula, the Bishop’s Sister (in Persian Church of the East (early))

items.quote: a claim that appears in this literature repeatedly and that modern historians treat as the martyr-genre's stock explanation rather than a record
items.heart: Tarbula and her companions were sawn apart on a charge of sorcery, and the Jewish accusation is a genre convention, not a fact.
items.why: The piece names "modern historians" and their treatment of the Jewish accusation, and the heart rests on this.

items.quote: the charge against 'the Jews' is a genre convention, not a corroborated fact
items.heart: Tarbula and her companions were sawn apart on a charge of sorcery, and the Jewish accusation is a genre convention, not a fact.
items.why: The verdict "a genre convention, not a corroborated fact" is a modern scholarly judgment told as settled, and it is the heart's own claim.

items.quote: The Jewish framing is part of that inheritance too, and the Church of the East, like the Greek and Latin churches, carried it forward without examination.
items.heart: Tarbula and her companions were sawn apart on a charge of sorcery, and the Jewish accusation is a genre convention, not a fact.
items.why: "Carried it forward without examination" is the narrator's judgment on later church reception, an aside to the heart.

name: The Lay Brothers of Schönau Refuse to Work (in Cistercian Monasticism)

items.quote: where the lay brothers rose against the abbot
items.heart: Cistercian lay brothers did the farm work, had no voice, and repeatedly revolted, and the order's own records preserve their complaints.

items.quote: at Eberbach in 1261 the conversi drove the abbot out
items.heart: Cistercian lay brothers did the farm work, had no voice, and repeatedly revolted, and the order's own records preserve their complaints.

items.quote: at Margam in Wales in 1206 they pursued the abbot on horseback and barricaded themselves in the dormitory
items.heart: Cistercian lay brothers did the farm work, had no voice, and repeatedly revolted, and the order's own records preserve their complaints.

name: Ten Years to a Verdict (in The Haugean Awakening)

items.quote: the high court reduced the sentence to a fine and costs
items.heart: The state's long case against Hauge ended in 1813-14 with a hard-labor sentence cut to a fine, and his movement outlasted him.
items.why: The cut from hard labor to a fine is the heart's own ending, and the piece gives no reason the high court reduced it.

items.quote: The Antonian movement of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita, from 1704 to 1706, falls inside this window.
items.heart: Kongo Christianity lived on after 1650 through Capuchin missions and local pride, with gaps in the record.

items.quote: a way of life he calls the most beastly of all
items.heart: Kongo Christianity lived on after 1650 through Capuchin missions and local pride, with gaps in the record.
items.why: The Jaga way of life is judged "most beastly" but the piece never says what it was.

items.quote: John Thornton's study of 1998 treats it, and how far it grew from the older church rests on that one study.
items.heart: Kongo Christianity after 1650 is seen through Capuchin friars' own books, with large gaps, and an Antonian movement of 1704 to 1706 known mainly from one study.
items.why: A modern scholar's 1998 study is named as the one basis for the Antonian movement, which the heart itself says is known mainly from one study.

name: Nine O'Clock in the Morning (in Charismatic Renewal & the Jesus Movement)

items.quote: Over the winter perhaps seventy of his parishioners followed.
items.heart: Bennett told his congregation in 1960 that he had spoken in tongues, resigned, and the press coverage made it a beginning.

items.quote: it was the coverage that made it a beginning
items.heart: Bennett told his congregation in 1960 that he had spoken in tongues, resigned, and the press coverage made it a beginning.
items.why: The causal claim that the coverage made it a beginning is the narrator's interpretation, and the heart rests on it.

name: The Bohohlasnyk at Pochaiv (in The Ruthenian Uniate Church — Zamość to the Partitions)

items.quote: passed across the confessional line into Orthodox use after 1839

items.heart: Josephus was a priest from Jerusalem who commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee when the Jews rose against Rome. In 67 he gave himself up to the Roman general Vespasian, and he spent the rest of his life at Rome, under the emperors' favour, writing his people's history (E1, E2, E6, S5; Documented, almost all from his own books). In his *Antiquities of the Jews*, finished about 93, he wrote a few lines each on John the Baptist, on James "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", and on Jesus himself (E11–E14; the John and James lines Widely Accepted as his). Christians kept and quoted those lines for centuries as a witness from outside the church. The passage on Jesus is the one they argued over. It has been disputed since the sixteenth century, an editor wrote in 1890 (EH-ed 9182–9185). Whether he wrote it as it stands is **Contested** (D2).

In 484 he led a synod, a council of bishops, at Beth Lapat against the catholicos, the head of his own church, and later took it back in writing (E5, E8, E10; Documented, his own letters). Yet what his side stood for became the Church of the East's settled law: clergy, the church's ordained ministers, free to marry, allowed in 486 and, in 497, accepted from Beth Lapat "only on this point"; and Theodore of Mopsuestia, a Greek Bible teacher, as its sure guide, confirmed in 605 (E11, I2, I3; Documented, the church's own synods). items.heart: Hippolytus was a Greek-writing teacher and elder of the church at Rome in the early two hundreds (S1, S2; Documented). In his *Refutation of All Heresies*, written after 222, he attacked Callistus, bishop of Rome from 217, as a man who forgave sinners too easily and who shared the teaching that Father and Son were one and the same (E4, E6, E7, E9; Documented as his charge; what Callistus taught, Contested). In 235 he was sent into exile on the island of Sardinia together with Pontianus, the bishop of Rome (E11; Documented, the list of 354; that the exile is this Hippolytus, Widely Accepted; that he was set to work in the mines is the historians' reading, DUH 11685–11686, EUS 35698–35700). In those years Babai, abbot (head) of the Great Monastery on Mount Izla near Nisibis, a monk and not a bishop, went round the church's monasteries for its senior bishops. He tested what the monks believed and drove out those the bishops judged heretics, people teaching what the church had condemned (E5; Documented as Thomas's account, about 840). He wrote the *Book of the Union*, on how Christ is one person who is both fully God and fully human, and his church kept and honoured his books (E6, I1; the books' keeping Documented; that his writing settled his church's teaching on Christ is the judgment of modern historians, Dominant Modern Reconstruction).

Soon after, he wrote *The Life and Passion of Cyprian*, so that Cyprian's example would reach later generations (E8; Documented, his own words; written about 259, Dominant Modern Reconstruction). It tells a bishop's life from his baptism to his death; a leading historian called it the oldest Christian biography that survives, and others call it a speech of praise (I3; Contested). The church's Bible was then in Latin, and English Scripture needed a bishop's leave (S3). Barred from the work at home, he had it printed abroad, at Worms on the Rhine in 1526, and smuggled into England (M3, M6: Widely Accepted, a diary's hearsay and the editor). There the bishop of London, the church's chief officer for the city, ordered every copy handed in, and the king ordered them burned (M8: Documented). Hunted by the king's agents, he was betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, and in 1536 he was strangled while tied to a post, and his body burned (M12, M16, M17: Documented to Widely Accepted; the manner is Foxe's account, D3).

Two years later he was made abbot of a new house, Clairvaux, and from there, by his sermons and his letters to popes, he became, in the tree's own words, the most listened-to churchman in Europe; popes and kings asked his word (S4, S6, E5, E6; Documented; "most listened-to" is the tree's own judgment, Widely Accepted).

items.quote: a bishop of Rome took their churches and drove their bishop into private houses

items.heart: Novatian was a leading elder of the church at Rome and a writer on the faith; his *On the Trinity* set out what the church believed of Father, Son and Spirit (E2; the book Documented; "leading" Widely Accepted, from Cornelius's sneer and Harnack, E2, E5). In 251 a stricter party made him a rival bishop of Rome against Cornelius, and he led a church that would not take back to communion those who had denied the faith under persecution; it left their pardon to God (E5, E8; Documented). That church lasted for centuries, and almost all we know of him comes from the men who fought him (S3, I1, I2; Witness kinds; Documented).

items.quote: An American historian who edited the record calls the refusal and the drunkenness slander.
items.heart: Novatian, a Roman elder and writer, was set up in 251 as rival bishop by a stricter party that would not take back the fallen, and is known almost only through the men who fought him.

items.quote: At Oxford in 1554 Cranmer was condemned for teaching what the church held false
items.flagged_by: B only (A was the earlier scan)
items.heart: Thomas Cranmer was archbishop of Canterbury from 1533 under Henry VIII, and under the boy king Edward VI he led the making of the Book of Common Prayer of 1549 and 1552, which put the church's services into English and gave the whole realm one form of worship (S3, E3, E7–E9, E11; Documented for the books and the office; that he led their making, Widely Accepted, the census and his editor); under Elizabeth his book of 1552 became the book of 1559, and it went on to shape worship in English (I1; CLAY 431–437, 443; census tradition `legacy`; Documented for 1559 from 1552, Widely Accepted for the wider legacy). Under the Catholic queen Mary he signed a series of recantations, then at Oxford in 1556 publicly took them back and was burned; Foxe, the Protestant writer who collected the stories of those burned under Mary, tells that he put into the fire first the hand that had signed them (E17, E20, E22, E24; the recantations and their withdrawal, Documented, his enemies' own print and register; the hand, Documented as Foxe's account).
items.why: The condemnation names no actual teaching, only "what the church held false," so the charge is empty, and the recantation in the heart turns on it.

items.quote: In June 1520 the pope's decree condemned his books, ordered them burned and gave him sixty days to take them back.
items.heart: Martin Luther, a friar (a member of a religious order under vows) who taught theology at Wittenberg, taught that forgiveness is God's free gift, received by trusting God's promise, not earned or bought (G1–G3: Documented, his own words of 1517, 1518 and 1520). So in 1517 he protested against the sale of indulgences, letters of pardon said to cancel punishment for sin, even for the dead (M1, M2, S5: Documented). Condemned by the pope, he would not take back his books before the emperor at Worms in 1521 unless Scripture or clear reason proved him wrong (M5, M7: Documented; "Here I stand" is Contested, D1). Outlawed and hidden, he put the New Testament into German (M9–M11: Documented). The churches that grew from his protest, the Lutheran churches, carry his name (CEN; I4: Documented).

Arrested in the Great Persecution, he wrote a Defense of Origen in prison, working with his pupil and friend Eusebius, and was put to death for his faith about 310 (E7, E8, E11; Documented, Eusebius's own account).

items.quote: Later councils, from 680 to 787, listed Evagrius with Origen and Didymus as condemned at Constantinople in 553.

Long after his death, councils named him with Origen among the condemned, yet monks in the Latin West and the Syriac East went on using what he taught.

items.heart: Patrick, a Briton from a Roman family, was carried off to Ireland as a slave at about sixteen. He escaped after six years. Years later he went back of his own will as a bishop, a senior church leader who could appoint other ministers, to the people who had enslaved him (E1, E3, E5, E7, E13; Documented, his own words). Almost all we know of him comes from his own two short Latin writings: the Confession, his account of his life and his thanks to God, and a letter against the soldiers of a warlord named Coroticus. They are the only words that survive from the first church in Ireland (I1; Documented that they are his and were kept; "only words" Widely Accepted, the census and White).

Almost everything known of him comes from the men who wrote against him (I3, E8–E12; Documented).

items.heart: Cyril was bishop of Alexandria, the head of the church in Egypt's great city, from 412 to 444. He taught that Christ is one: God's own Son, whom the Bible calls the Word, was himself born of Mary as a man, so she may rightly be called Mother of God, the one who gave birth to God (E4: Documented, his own words). He led the attack on Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, which ended with a council of bishops at Ephesus in 431 removing Nestorius from office (E6: Documented). His twelve short statements of faith, each cursing those who denied it, and his phrase "one incarnate nature of God the Word", meaning one Christ, God become man and never divided, became the test of true faith for the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia that later refused the Council of Chalcedon (I1, I2: Documented for Egypt and Syria; Armenia from the census Chalcedon text, I4). Chalcedon, the council of 451 that said Christ is known in two natures, fully God and fully human, also took his letters as a guide (I4: Documented).

items.quote: when a rival bishop came in 339 he fled to Rome
items.asks: Why did a rival bishop come, and why did he flee?
items.flagged_by: B only (A was the earlier scan)
items.heart: For forty-five years Athanasius was bishop, the church's leader, in Alexandria. He held to the creed of Nicaea, the statement of faith bishops agreed in 325: that the Son is "of one being" with the Father, fully God as the Father is. He held it against the party of Arius, who taught that the Son had a beginning. For Athanasius the word mattered because of what God had done: God's Son became human so that human beings might be made divine, joined to God and freed from death. That could happen, he wrote, only if the Son were truly God (T1, T2; Documented, his own words). Five times he had to leave his city, by order or in flight (S1, S2, E4–E13; Documented each time; the count of five is Widely Accepted, D2). In those years he wrote the *Life of Antony*, the story of an Egyptian hermit, which carried the desert monks' way of life to readers abroad. And in 367, in the yearly letter that set the date of Easter, he listed the books to be read as Scripture, with the twenty-seven of the New Testament (E11, E14; the letter Documented; the *Life* as his work Widely Accepted, D1).
items.why: The piece never says who set up the rival bishop in 339, or why, so this exile has no cause.

items.quote: A philosopher at Rome, he adds, tried to have both Justin and him put to death.
items.asks: Why did he want them killed?
items.heart: Tatian, a man born "in the land of the Assyrians" and trained in Greek learning, became a Christian at Rome and a hearer of Justin. In his *Address to the Greeks* he turned on everything he had studied: their gods, their philosophers and their arts, all borrowed, he said, from the peoples they called barbarians, and all younger than Moses (S2, E3, E5; Documented, his own words). After Justin's death he broke with the church, by the account of his opponent Irenaeus, about 172 by Eusebius's date (E6, S4; Documented as Irenaeus's account and Eusebius's date). He went back east, and his *Diatessaron*, the four Gospels woven into one continuous story, became for about two centuries the gospel most Syriac-speaking churches heard read (E7, E8, I1; the journey east Widely Accepted, resting on Epiphanius two centuries later; the harmony's use Documented; "very widely if not universally read" is Hogg's judgment, Widely Accepted).

items.flagged_by: B only (A was the earlier scan)
items.heart: Around the year 112, Pliny, a Roman man of letters governing the province of Bithynia on the Black Sea, was trying people accused of being Christians, and having those who would not deny it led away to be punished. Unsure of the law, he wrote to the emperor Trajan to ask what to do (S2, S5, E2; Documented, his own letter; that those "led away" died is the later writers' reading, Widely Accepted). His letter and Trajan's short reply are a Roman judge's own record of the church on trial: how he tested them, what people who had left the faith told him of their worship before dawn, and the emperor's rule that Christians were not to be hunted out, but punished if they were accused and would not deny it (E5, E7, E11; Documented).
items.why: The ban on private clubs is said to come on Trajan's orders, but no reason for it is given.

items.quote: In 1540 Geneva's councils wrote begging him back.
items.asks: Why did they want him back?
items.heart: John Calvin was a French scholar in exile. He wrote the Institutes, a book of instruction in the Christian faith, first to defend the Protestants being burned in France. Passing through Geneva for one night in 1536, he was held there. He gave the city a written plan for running its church: pastors to preach, teachers, deacons to care for the poor and sick, and elders, laymen who watched over people's lives. Elders and pastors met each week as the consistory, a church court. Protestant churches in France and Scotland built their own churches on that plan, and his name became the label for the whole family.
items.why: The councils beg for Calvin's return two years after expelling him, and the piece gives no reason for the change.

items.heart: Catherine of Siena, a dyer's daughter who never entered a convent, gathered a circle of followers and dictated letters to popes, cities and rulers (S1, E1-E3; Documented). In 1376 she went to Avignon and pressed Gregory XI to take the papacy back to Rome, and that September he left for Rome (E7-E11; Documented). How far she moved him is disputed: her confessor says she led him to it, while her own letters show he had already decided, and later writers gave other causes (D1-D3; Contested).
items.why: The envoys' refusal to deal with her is stated with no reason, and the piece spends little time on the peace mission.

items.quote: The bishop of Caesarea made him a priest, though they quarreled.
items.heart: Basil of Caesarea gave up teaching rhetoric for a life of prayer and shared work. He wrote the rules that taught monks to live together and serve one another, built a great lodging for the poor and the sick a little way outside Caesarea, and as its bishop from 370 defended the Holy Spirit's place beside the Father and the Son. He died in 378 or 379, before the council of 381 confessed it.

items.heart: Damasus was bishop of Rome from 366 to 384. He won the office in an election fought with clubs and killing. He then held his church to the faith of Nicaea, and in 380 the emperors' law named him as that faith's standard. *(Election: AMM 23176–23189, Documented; the clubs: AVE 5107, 5159, the Ursinian account, Contested; the dates: S1, S4, E53, Dominant Modern Reconstruction; the law: CTH 83598–83601, Documented.)*

items.quote: the churches of Egypt and Syria refused it
items.asks: Why did they refuse the Tome?
items.heart: Leo, bishop of Rome from 440 to 461, wrote the letter called the Tome in 449 to say how Christ is one person, fully God and fully human; two years later the Council of Chalcedon took it as its rule of faith (E7, E17, E18, I1; Documented). He held that Peter still spoke and ruled through the bishop of Rome, and he would not accept the council's canon that ranked Constantinople next to Rome (E3, E21, E22; Documented, his own words).
items.why: The refusal by the churches of Egypt and Syria is stated with no reason.

items.quote: A council deposed the patriarch
items.heart: Gregory Palamas, a monk of Mount Athos, defended the hesychasts, the monks of stillness, when the scholar Barlaam mocked their silent prayer and the light they said they saw (E2, E7; Documented as Kantakouzenos's account and Palamas's own words). He taught that God cannot be shared in his essence, yet gives himself truly in his uncreated energy, so that one who is joined to God is joined to God himself (E8, E9; Documented, his own words; that this is true, the councils' verdict, contested by his opponents, D2).

items.quote: An editor of his sermons writes that a list read aloud in churches on the first Sunday of Lent acclaims his name every year.

items.why: A modern editor of the sermons is cited for the Lenten acclamation, in passing.

items.heart: When Alexander of Alexandria put Arius out, Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, the city where the emperor lived, took up Arius's cause (SOC 2123-2126, 2381-2391). After a short exile that followed Nicaea, he led the bishops who drove Arius's opponents from their churches, and he died bishop of Constantinople (SOC 4662-4668, 5885-5890, 6175-6177). Nearly everything we know of him was written by his enemies (Source_Sheet §5.1). Documented.
